title: Precalculus: Functions, Models, and Change
subtitle: Functions, Models, and Change
description: A continuous Precalculus course built around functions, multiple representations, exact reasoning, modeling, and change.

units.title: Algebra and Function Readiness
units.description: A readiness diagnostic separates prerequisite strands so that a learner receives targeted repair rather than one vague total score.
outcomes: Use diagnostic evidence to identify which prerequisite strands are secure and which require targeted repair.
Classify and solve common equation and inequality families while distinguishing reversible steps from candidate-generating steps.
Recognize and apply the principal factoring structures needed for polynomial-function analysis.
Simplify and solve rational expressions while preserving every restriction from the original form.
Move among radical and rational-exponent forms, simplify exact values, and reject extraneous candidates.
Apply exponent and logarithm laws, convert between inverse forms, and solve basic equations with valid domains.
Evaluate functions, solve output conditions, and read domain, range, intercepts, extrema, and intervals from graphs.
Select methods across prerequisite strands, justify restrictions, and communicate exact and approximate results.

units.title: Functions and Multiple Representations
units.description: An input is supplied to a relationship, an output is determined by it, and parameters remain fixed for one selected model.
outcomes: Identify the input, output, parameters, and units in a quantitative relationship and explain how the quantities depend on one another.
Determine whether a relation is a function by applying the rule that each allowed input has exactly one output.
Use function notation accurately and distinguish finding an output from finding inputs that produce a chosen output.
Translate a function relationship among verbal, tabular, graphical, and algebraic representations while preserving quantities, units, and domain.
Determine the real domain of a function by combining denominator, even-root, logarithm, and composition restrictions.
Distinguish the algebraic domain of a formula from the inputs that are meaningful in a model.
Read range, intercepts, extrema, boundedness, symmetry, and intervals of increase or decrease from a graph.
Evaluate, graph, and interpret functions that use different rules on different parts of the domain.
Calculate and interpret average rate of change as output change per input change and as the slope of a secant line.
Construct, compare, and defend function representations while stating assumptions, domain, units, and limitations.

Build a multi-stage function model, state its domain and assumptions, and evaluate whether an inverse interpretation is meaningful.

Relate the multiplicity of a zero to sign changes, crossing or touching behavior, and local flattening.

Use polynomial continuity and sign changes to guarantee roots and bracket them within intervals.
Divide polynomials using long and synthetic division and verify the division algorithm P=DQ+R.
Use P(c) as the remainder on division by x-c and test whether x-c is a factor.

Count polynomial zeros over the complex numbers, use conjugate pairs for real coefficients, and build real polynomials from complex roots.
Construct polynomial functions from conditions, fit vertical scale, and approximate roots that lack convenient exact forms.

lessons.title: Quantities, variables, and dependency
lessons.outcome: Identify the input, output, parameters, and units in a quantitative relationship and explain how the quantities depend on one another.
opening: An input is supplied to a relationship, an output is determined by it, and parameters remain fixed for one selected model.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use quantities, variables, and dependency to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
prerequisites: Use function notation from the algebra and function readiness unit.
Read ordered pairs and interval notation.
exposition: Define every quantity and unit, identify the direction of dependency, and check that terms combined in a formula have compatible units.
The same symbol can play different roles in different models; the context determines whether it is input, output, or parameter.
A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through quantity dependency map, parameter family graph, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: The same dependency may arrive as a story, table, graph, or formula. Learning to preserve the inputs, outputs, units, and domain while moving among those forms is the central language of the course.
bigIdea: A function is a dependency, not merely an equation. Inputs, outputs, units, and domain must agree in words, tables, graphs, and formulas; each representation should tell the same mathematical story.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: identify the input, output, parameters, and units in a quantitative relationship and explain how the quantities depend on one another. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Define every quantity.
2. Unit.
3. Identify the direction of dependency.
4. Check that terms combined in a formula have compatible units.
questions: What is the input and what is the output?
Which inputs are allowed?
Where is the same feature visible in another representation?
guide.verification: Choose two representations and make them verify one another. A table can test a formula, a graph can expose a domain or range claim, and units can reveal a model that is algebraically neat but conceptually wrong.

lessons.title: Products and quotients of functions
lessons.outcome: Multiply and divide functions pointwise while analyzing zeros, restrictions, and combined graph behavior.
opening: Product functions multiply outputs; quotient functions divide outputs and exclude every denominator-function zero.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use products and quotients of functions to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.

exposition: Intersect domains, factor, locate product zeros, add quotient restrictions, and use signs to analyze the graph.

guide.application: Transformation language lets you read a complicated graph as a modified parent rather than a collection of disconnected points. That makes prediction possible before any calculator window is opened.
bigIdea: Transformations become reliable when they are treated as coordinate mappings. Outside operations change outputs; inside operations change the inputs that produce those outputs, which is why horizontal changes often appear to work in the opposite direction.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: multiply and divide functions pointwise while analyzing zeros, restrictions, and combined graph behavior. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.

lessons.title: Composition as sequential processing
lessons.outcome: Interpret f composed with g as applying g first and then f, and explain why order generally matters.
opening: Composition represents an ordered chain in which the inner function acts first.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use composition as sequential processing to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
prerequisites: Solve equations for a selected variable.
exposition: Trace the original input through the first function, name the intermediate quantity, and feed it to the second function.
The intermediate output must lie in the outer function's domain and have compatible units.
A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through two-stage machine, order comparison, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Many real models are built in stages—a conversion followed by a cost rule, or a measurement followed by a calibration. Composition records that order, while inverse reasoning asks whether the stages can be undone.
bigIdea: Composition and inversion are about information flow. A composite sends an input through stages in a fixed order; an inverse reverses that flow only when each output identifies a unique input.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: interpret f composed with g as applying g first and then f, and explain why order generally matters. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Trace the original input through the first function.
2. Name the intermediate quantity.
3. Feed it to the second function.
questions: Which function acts first?
Is the intermediate output allowed?
Can the process be reversed without ambiguity?
guide.verification: Name the intermediate quantity, enforce its domain, and verify an inverse with composition. Units are especially useful because the output unit of one stage must match the input unit of the next.

lessons.title: Graphs and verification of inverses

lessons.title: Rational-root candidates and root search
lessons.outcome: Generate all possible rational zeros of an integer-coefficient polynomial and organize an efficient exact-and-numerical search.
opening: The Rational Root Theorem produces a finite list of possible rational zeros p/q.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use rational-root candidates and root search to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
exposition: Let p divide the constant term and q divide the leading coefficient, reduce all signed ratios, and test candidates exactly.
The theorem limits rational possibilities only; irrational and complex roots may remain.
A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through rational-root lattice, candidate workflow, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Polynomial structure links symbolic factors to visible graph behavior. Reading that structure efficiently makes it possible to sketch, solve, and model without treating every problem as a blind numerical search.
bigIdea: Polynomial formulas contain structural information before a graph is drawn. Degree and leading coefficient control the ends, factors reveal zeros, multiplicity predicts crossing or touching, and selected values settle the remaining shape.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: generate all possible rational zeros of an integer-coefficient polynomial and organize an efficient exact-and-numerical search. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Let p divide the constant term.
2. Q divide the leading coefficient.
3. Reduce all signed ratios.
4. Test candidates exactly.
questions: What does the leading term force at the ends?
Where are the zeros and what are their multiplicities?
Which intervals are positive or negative?
guide.verification: Compare the proposed graph with the factorization and leading term. Every real zero, sign interval, end direction, and y-intercept should agree with the same formula.

lessons.title: Rational functions and their domains
lessons.outcome: Identify rational functions and determine all excluded inputs from the original denominator before simplifying.
opening: A rational function P/Q excludes every real input where the original denominator Q is zero.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use rational functions and their domains to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
exposition: Factor the denominator, solve Q=0, record exclusions, and partition the domain into intervals of continuity.
A rational function can have all-real domain when its denominator has no real zero.
A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through numerator-denominator role map, domain intervals, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Rational graphs are organized around the inputs the denominator forbids. Those exclusions divide the graph into continuity intervals and explain why a simplified expression may still contain a hole or asymptote.
bigIdea: A rational function carries permanent memory of its original denominator. Factoring may reveal holes, asymptotes, and sign changes, but cancellation never restores an input that the original formula excluded.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: identify rational functions and determine all excluded inputs from the original denominator before simplifying. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Factor the denominator.
2. Solve Q=0.
3. Record exclusions.
4. Partition the domain into intervals of continuity.
questions: Which inputs make the original denominator zero?
Does each excluded input create a hole or an asymptote?
What happens on each continuity interval?
guide.verification: Record exclusions first, then compare the factored and simplified forms. Test one point in every sign interval and examine both sides of each vertical asymptote.

lessons.title: Equivalent formulas, different functions, and holes
lessons.outcome: Identify removable discontinuities caused by common factors and distinguish formula equivalence from function equality.
opening: A common factor creates a removable discontinuity: the original function follows the simplified curve but omits one point.

This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use equivalent formulas, different functions, and holes to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
exposition: Factor, retain original exclusions, cancel, and evaluate the simplified formula at the cancelled input to locate the hole.
Two formulas define the same function only when both domains and values match.

A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through cancellation with domain memory, hole coordinate construction, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Rational graphs are organized around the inputs the denominator forbids. Those exclusions divide the graph into continuity intervals and explain why a simplified expression may still contain a hole or asymptote.
bigIdea: A rational function carries permanent memory of its original denominator. Factoring may reveal holes, asymptotes, and sign changes, but cancellation never restores an input that the original formula excluded.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: identify removable discontinuities caused by common factors and distinguish formula equivalence from function equality. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Factor.
2. Retain original exclusions.
3. Cancel.
4. Evaluate the simplified formula at the cancelled input to locate the hole.
questions: Which inputs make the original denominator zero?
Does each excluded input create a hole or an asymptote?
What happens on each continuity interval?
guide.verification: Record exclusions first, then compare the factored and simplified forms. Test one point in every sign interval and examine both sides of each vertical asymptote.

lessons.title: Additive versus multiplicative change

opening: Constant first differences indicate additive linear change; constant ratios indicate multiplicative exponential change.

exposition: Compare equal input steps, compute differences and ratios, and convert percentage rates to multipliers.
Noisy data suggest a candidate family rather than proving one.

A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through difference-ratio comparison, additive-multiplicative timelines, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Multiplicative models describe repeated percentage change, while logarithms recover the time or exponent hidden inside that process. Together they support growth, decay, finance, regression, and bounded models.
bigIdea: Exponential change multiplies over equal input steps, while logarithms answer the inverse question: what exponent produces a given output? Parameters must be interpreted as an initial value, a multiplier, a rate, or a long-run bound—not as decoration.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: distinguish linear, exponential, and neither patterns by comparing equal-input differences, ratios, and percent changes. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.

lessons.title: Solving exponential equations
lessons.outcome: Solve exponential equations using common bases, logarithms, and numerical methods, and interpret exact and approximate answers.
opening: Exponential equations place the unknown in an exponent and are solved by common bases, logarithms, substitution, or numerical methods.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use solving exponential equations to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
exposition: Isolate the exponential, choose a common-base or logarithmic path, retain exact form, approximate at the end, and check the model domain.
Positive-base exponentials have positive outputs; sums of exponentials may require a new variable.
A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through equation method tree, taking logs steps, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Multiplicative models describe repeated percentage change, while logarithms recover the time or exponent hidden inside that process. Together they support growth, decay, finance, regression, and bounded models.
bigIdea: Exponential change multiplies over equal input steps, while logarithms answer the inverse question: what exponent produces a given output? Parameters must be interpreted as an initial value, a multiplier, a rate, or a long-run bound—not as decoration.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: solve exponential equations using common bases, logarithms, and numerical methods, and interpret exact and approximate answers. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Isolate the exponential.
2. Choose a common-base or logarithmic path.
3. Retain exact form.
4. Approximate at the end.
questions: Is change additive, multiplicative, or bounded?
What do the parameters mean with units?
Would a logarithm reverse the relationship?
guide.verification: Test the model at input zero and one step later, confirm the multiplier or inverse relationship, and state whether the domain and long-run behavior make sense in context.

lessons.title: Systems as intersections and models
lessons.outcome: Interpret a system solution as an input-output point satisfying every equation and solve two-variable systems graphically and algebraically.
opening: A system solution satisfies every equation simultaneously and appears graphically as a common intersection.
This matters because the rest of Precalculus will repeatedly use systems as intersections and models to decide what a formula means, what a graph can show, and which conclusions remain valid.
exposition: Choose graphing, substitution, or elimination from the visible structure and verify the ordered pair in every equation.
Parallel lines have no solution and coincident lines have infinitely many solutions.

A symbolic answer is not complete by itself. In this lesson, the same claim must also be readable through system representation triangle, line solution-count gallery, or another equivalent representation.

guide.application: Systems combine several conditions into one decision. Graphs, equations, inequalities, and matrices are different views of the same requirement: the final result must satisfy every condition at once.
bigIdea: A system asks for simultaneous truth. Graphs show common intersections, elimination preserves the solution set, and matrices record the same operations compactly; the representation changes, but the solution condition does not.

This lesson narrows that lens to one goal: interpret a system solution as an input-output point satisfying every equation and solve two-variable systems graphically and algebraically. The point is not to memorize an isolated trick; it is to know what evidence makes the conclusion valid and how a second representation can check it.
method: 1. Choose graphing.
2. Substitution.
3. Or elimination from the visible structure.
4. Verify the ordered pair in every equation.
questions: What does a solution represent in this context?
Which elimination move preserves the solution set?
Does the result satisfy every original condition?
guide.verification: Substitute the result into every original equation or inequality. For matrix work, translate the final rows back into statements about variables, pivots, free variables, and consistency.

lessons.title: Systems of inequalities and feasible regions

opening: A system of inequalities describes the intersection of several shaded solution regions.

lessons.title: Directed rotation and coterminal angles
lessons.outcome: Represent rotations in standard position and generate all coterminal angles.
opening: A radar arm begins on the positive x-axis, rotates 765 degrees counterclockwise, then 180 degrees clockwise. Where is its terminal side, and what is the smallest positive coterminal angle?
Directed rotations appear in navigation, rotating machinery, phase, circular motion, and complex-number arguments.
exposition: A directed angle records rotation from an initial ray to a terminal ray. Counterclockwise rotation is positive and clockwise rotation is negative. Angles that end on the same terminal ray are coterminal.

The same terminal side can be reached after any whole number of revolutions. In degrees, one revolution adds 360 degrees; in radians, it adds 2pi. This means an angle is not determined by its terminal side alone: 45 degrees, 405 degrees, and -315 degrees describe different rotations with the same final direction.

To reduce an angle, add or subtract complete revolutions until the value lies in the desired interval. The operation changes the accumulated rotation but preserves the terminal side because every full revolution returns the ray to its prior direction.

lessons.title: Degree measure and angular coordinates
lessons.outcome: Use degrees, revolutions, and degree-minute-second notation to measure and compare rotation.
opening: A telescope turns from heading 18 degrees 42 minutes to heading 137 degrees 15 minutes. Through what angle did it rotate?
DMS is useful when measurements are recorded with angular precision smaller than one degree.
exposition: Degree measure partitions one full revolution into 360 equal parts. A degree may be subdivided into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds.

The degree system is historically convenient and remains common in surveying, navigation, astronomy, and everyday communication. Standard-position angles begin at the positive x-axis, but navigation headings commonly begin at north and increase clockwise, so the convention must always be named.

Degree-minute-second notation is a base-60 place-value system. To convert to decimal degrees, divide minutes by 60 and seconds by 3600. To reverse the conversion, separate the whole degrees and repeatedly multiply the fractional part by 60.

lessons.title: Radian measure as normalized arc length
lessons.outcome: Define radian measure as signed arc length divided by radius and explain why it is independent of circle size.
opening: Two circles have radii 2 and 10. On each, an arc has length equal to three times the radius. What angle does each arc subtend?
Radians simplify arc length, angular speed, trigonometric graphs, derivatives, and periodic models.
exposition: The radian measure of a central angle is the signed arc length it intercepts divided by the circle radius: theta=s/r.

Because both s and r scale together, their ratio is independent of the size of the circle. An angle of one radian cuts off an arc whose length equals the radius. A full circle has arc length 2pi r, so a full revolution measures 2pi radians.

Radians convert circular geometry into ordinary real-number input. On the unit circle, radius one makes the numerical angle equal to signed arc length. This is why radians are the natural input for trigonometric functions and later Calculus formulas.

guide.application: Radians simplify arc length, angular speed, trigonometric graphs, derivatives, and periodic models.

method: 1. Use theta=s/r to compute angle, and use the identity 180 degrees=pi radians for conversion. Exact radian answers should retain pi when the angle is a rational part of a revolution.
2. The formula assumes s and r use the same length unit. Radian measure is dimensionless, though writing “rad” can clarify interpretation.

opening: A sprinkler waters a sector of radius 12 meters through an angle of 5pi/12. Find the boundary arc length and watered area.

lessons.title: Angular speed and linear speed
lessons.outcome: Relate angular speed, radius, and tangential speed using v=r omega.
opening: A bicycle wheel has radius 0.34 meter and turns at 180 revolutions per minute. Find angular speed in radians per second and bicycle speed in meters per second.
The relation supports wheel speedometers, pulleys, gears, turbines, turntables, and orbital motion.
exposition: Angular speed omega measures angle change per unit time, while tangential speed v measures distance traveled along a circular path per unit time. They satisfy v=r omega when omega is in radians per time.

Every point on a rigid rotating body sweeps the same angle during the same time interval. Points farther from the axis travel longer arcs, so their linear speeds are larger even though their angular speeds match.

The formula follows from s=r theta: divide both sides by elapsed time to obtain s/t=r(theta/t). In a belt or no-slip contact, connected rims share tangential speed even when their radii and angular speeds differ.

guide.application: The relation supports wheel speedometers, pulleys, gears, turbines, turntables, and orbital motion.
bigIdea: Angular speed omega measures angle change per unit time, while tangential speed v measures distance traveled along a circular path per unit time. They satisfy v=r omega when omega is in radians per time.

Every point on a rigid rotating body sweeps the same angle during the same time interval. Points farther from the axis travel longer arcs, so their linear speeds are larger even though their angular speeds match.
method: 1. Convert rotations per time to radians per time before using v=r omega. Track time units carefully and decide whether the problem asks for angular or linear speed.
2. The no-slip relationship assumes the rim and belt or surface move together. Slipping, deformation, and changing radius require a different model.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Wrapping the real line around the unit circle
lessons.outcome: Map any real number t to the unit-circle point reached by signed arc length t.
opening: Starting at (1,0), where does traveling an arc length of 17pi/6 counterclockwise place the point?
This construction is the bridge from geometric circles to real-valued periodic functions.
exposition: The wrapping function maps a real number t to the point reached by traveling signed arc length t around the unit circle from (1,0).

Since the unit circle has circumference 2pi, inputs differing by 2pi k reach the same point. This gives a many-to-one map from the real line to the circle and creates the periodicity later inherited by sine and cosine.
Positive t moves counterclockwise and negative t moves clockwise. Reducing t modulo 2pi identifies a convenient coterminal input without changing the terminal point.

guide.application: This construction is the bridge from geometric circles to real-valued periodic functions.
bigIdea: The wrapping function maps a real number t to the point reached by traveling signed arc length t around the unit circle from (1,0).

Since the unit circle has circumference 2pi, inputs differing by 2pi k reach the same point. This gives a many-to-one map from the real line to the circle and creates the periodicity later inherited by sine and cosine.
method: 1. Reduce the input, locate the terminal side, use special-angle coordinates or geometry, and keep track of signs by quadrant.
2. The wrapping map is defined for every real t. The point is unique even though infinitely many inputs map to it.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Sine and cosine as coordinate functions
lessons.outcome: Define cosine and sine as the x- and y-coordinates of the unit-circle point P(t).
opening: A rotating point has unit-circle coordinate P(t)=(-5/13,12/13). Find sin t, cos t, and the quadrant.
Coordinate functions model circular position, oscillation, projection, sound, waves, and periodic change.
exposition: If P(t)=(x,y) is the unit-circle point associated with t, then cos t=x and sin t=y.

The definitions make sine and cosine functions of every real input. The identity x^2+y^2=1 becomes sin^2 t+cos^2 t=1. Coordinate signs give quadrant signs, and the coordinate bounds produce ranges [-1,1].
A known coordinate immediately gives sine and cosine. If one coordinate is known, use the unit-circle equation to find the other, then use the quadrant to choose the correct sign.

lessons.title: Exact values from special triangles
lessons.outcome: Derive exact unit-circle values from 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.
opening: Without using a memorized chart, derive sin(pi/3), cos(pi/3), and tan(pi/3).
These exact anchors support graph construction, identities, equations, vectors, and triangle solving.
exposition: Exact values at pi/6, pi/4, and pi/3 come from the side ratios of 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles scaled to hypotenuse one.

An isosceles right triangle with legs one has hypotenuse sqrt2, so unit scaling gives legs sqrt2/2. Halving an equilateral triangle gives side ratios 1:sqrt3:2, which scale to 1/2 and sqrt3/2 on the unit circle.
Once first-quadrant coordinates are derived, reflection symmetry places the same magnitudes in every quadrant with signs determined by coordinate location.

guide.application: These exact anchors support graph construction, identities, equations, vectors, and triangle solving.
bigIdea: Exact values at pi/6, pi/4, and pi/3 come from the side ratios of 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles scaled to hypotenuse one.

An isosceles right triangle with legs one has hypotenuse sqrt2, so unit scaling gives legs sqrt2/2. Halving an equilateral triangle gives side ratios 1:sqrt3:2, which scale to 1/2 and sqrt3/2 on the unit circle.
method: 1. Derive the triangle ratios rather than relying on a memorized wheel. Record coordinates as (cos t,sin t), then obtain tangent as their ratio when cosine is nonzero.
2. Exact values should remain radicals. Decimal approximations are useful for checking but obscure geometric structure.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Reference angles, quadrants, and signs
lessons.outcome: Use reference angles and quadrant signs to evaluate trigonometric functions of arbitrary rotations.
opening: Evaluate sin(23pi/6), cos(23pi/6), and tan(23pi/6) exactly.
The same reasoning later generates all solutions to trig equations.
exposition: A reference angle is the positive acute angle between a terminal side and the x-axis. It determines the magnitudes of trig values, while the quadrant determines their signs.

Reference angles separate two tasks: identify a familiar acute triangle and then restore the signs of the original coordinates. Coterminal reduction may be useful first, but a reference angle is not the same as a coterminal angle.
Reduce the angle if needed, identify the quadrant, find the acute distance to the nearest x-axis, evaluate the special-angle magnitude, and assign signs from the coordinate quadrant.

Reference angles separate two tasks: identify a familiar acute triangle and then restore the signs of the original coordinates. Coterminal reduction may be useful first, but a reference angle is not the same as a coterminal angle.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
Reduce the angle if needed, identify the quadrant, find the acute distance to the nearest x-axis, evaluate the special-angle magnitude, and assign signs from the coordinate quadrant.
Angles on the axes have no acute reference triangle and should be evaluated directly from their coordinates.
A common error is to report the reference angle as the original solution or to use an always-positive mnemonic that ignores tangent’s sign.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
Reference angles make exact evaluation possible for large, negative, and multi-revolution inputs.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Tangent and the reciprocal functions
lessons.outcome: Define tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant from sine and cosine and state domains, signs, periods, and identities.
opening: A unit-circle point is P=(-8/17,15/17). Find all six trig values and identify which are negative.
The six functions provide the language for slope, projection, triangles, identities, and periodic graphs.
exposition: Tangent and cotangent are coordinate ratios, while secant and cosecant are reciprocals: tan=sin/cos, cot=cos/sin, sec=1/cos, csc=1/sin.

The definitions make domain restrictions visible. Tangent and secant are undefined where cosine is zero; cotangent and cosecant are undefined where sine is zero. Tangent and cotangent repeat after pi because both numerator and denominator change sign after a half-turn.
The unit-circle identity produces two more identities by division: 1+tan^2 t=sec^2 t and cot^2 t+1=csc^2 t.

guide.application: The six functions provide the language for slope, projection, triangles, identities, and periodic graphs.
bigIdea: Tangent and cotangent are coordinate ratios, while secant and cosecant are reciprocals: tan=sin/cos, cot=cos/sin, sec=1/cos, csc=1/sin.

The definitions make domain restrictions visible. Tangent and secant are undefined where cosine is zero; cotangent and cosecant are undefined where sine is zero. Tangent and cotangent repeat after pi because both numerator and denominator change sign after a half-turn.
method: 1. Start with sine and cosine coordinates, form ratios and reciprocals, simplify exact radicals, and retain undefined cases.
2. A reciprocal trig function is not an inverse trig function. The notation sec t means 1/cos t, while arccos is the inverse function of a restricted cosine branch.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Building the sine graph from circular motion
lessons.outcome: Construct y=sin t from the vertical coordinate of a rotating unit-circle point.
opening: A point starts at (1,0) and rotates counterclockwise one revolution in 8 seconds. Sketch its vertical coordinate against time and label zeros, extrema, and period.
Sine models vertical projection, alternating current, sound, tides, and repeated motion.
exposition: The sine graph records the vertical coordinate of a unit-circle point as the real input t increases.

At quarter-turn intervals, sine moves through 0,1,0,-1,0. Connecting these values smoothly according to circular motion produces a periodic wave with range [-1,1], period 2pi, zeros at integer multiples of pi, and odd symmetry.
The graph is not an arbitrary wave. Every point (t,sin t) is paired with the same input’s position on the circle. The rising and falling portions correspond to the point moving upward or downward.

method: 1. Build a key-point table at multiples of pi/2, plot one cycle, use symmetry and periodicity to extend, and label zeros, extrema, and intervals of increase or decrease.
2. The input axis represents angle or time-scaled angle, not horizontal position on the circle.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Building the cosine graph from circular motion
lessons.outcome: Construct y=cos t from the horizontal coordinate of circular motion and compare it with sine.
opening: A rotating point begins at (1,0). At what inputs does its horizontal coordinate equal its vertical coordinate during one revolution?
Cosine naturally models quantities that begin at a maximum or minimum.
exposition: The cosine graph records the horizontal coordinate of unit-circle motion.

Cosine begins at 1, moves through 0,-1,0,1, and repeats every 2pi. It is even because the points reached at t and -t have the same horizontal coordinate. Cosine is a phase-shifted sine: cos t=sin(t+pi/2).
Comparing sine and cosine on the same axes reveals that they describe perpendicular projections of one rotating point rather than unrelated formulas.

Cosine begins at 1, moves through 0,-1,0,1, and repeats every 2pi. It is even because the points reached at t and -t have the same horizontal coordinate. Cosine is a phase-shifted sine: cos t=sin(t+pi/2).

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
Comparing sine and cosine on the same axes reveals that they describe perpendicular projections of one rotating point rather than unrelated formulas.
Construct cosine from unit-circle key points, identify its extrema and zeros, and compare its graph to sine by horizontal translation.
Equivalent phase-shift descriptions are not unique; adding whole periods produces the same function.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is to assume cosine has a different period or to shift in the wrong direction when rewriting it as sine.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Amplitude, reflection, and midline
lessons.outcome: Interpret A and D in y=A sin x+D or y=A cos x+D.
opening: An ocean buoy moves between 1.2 and 4.8 meters above a reference level. Find the midline and amplitude.
Amplitude and midline describe tides, temperatures, voltage, vibration, and circular height.
exposition: In y=A sin x+D or y=A cos x+D, |A| is the amplitude and y=D is the midline.
The maximum is D+|A| and the minimum is D-|A|. A negative A reflects the wave across its midline without making amplitude negative.
Amplitude is a distance, so it is nonnegative. The midline is the average of the maximum and minimum, and amplitude is half their difference.

guide.application: Amplitude and midline describe tides, temperatures, voltage, vibration, and circular height.
bigIdea: In y=A sin x+D or y=A cos x+D, |A| is the amplitude and y=D is the midline.
The maximum is D+|A| and the minimum is D-|A|. A negative A reflects the wave across its midline without making amplitude negative.
method: 1. Read extrema from a graph or context, compute D=(max+min)/2 and |A|=(max-min)/2, then use the sign of A to match the starting direction or phase.
2. This interpretation assumes a sinusoid with symmetric extrema about a constant midline.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Period, frequency, and angular frequency
lessons.outcome: Relate inside scale B to period, ordinary frequency, and angular frequency.
opening: A piston completes 15 cycles in 6 seconds. Find frequency, period, and angular frequency.
Frequency parameters model music, rotation, seasonal cycles, waves, and machinery.
exposition: For sin(Bx) or cos(Bx), the period is 2pi/|B|. Ordinary frequency is the reciprocal of period, while angular frequency measures radians per unit time.
The inside multiplier changes how quickly the input completes a full 2pi cycle. If B is larger, the graph completes more cycles in the same horizontal distance.
For a time model, angular frequency omega=2pi f=2pi/T. The units distinguish cycles per second, seconds per cycle, and radians per second.

method: 1. Identify the coefficient of the entire input, compute period, then convert to frequency or angular frequency as requested.
2. A model must state the input unit. A period of 12 could mean seconds, months, or meters.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Phase shift and timing
lessons.outcome: Interpret B(x-C) as a horizontal timing shift and recover C from graph or context.
opening: A seasonal temperature reaches its maximum on day 205 of a 365-day cycle. Write a cosine model phase term with the maximum at day 205.
Phase aligns a periodic model with calendar dates, starting positions, or delayed signals.
exposition: A phase shift relocates the timing of every feature of a periodic graph.
In B(x-C), the parent input is zero when x=C, so the graph’s anchor feature occurs at C. Factoring B from an expanded inside expression is necessary before reading the shift.
Sine and cosine forms can model the same cycle with different phase choices. The best form often places a known maximum, minimum, or midline crossing at a simple input.

guide.application: Phase aligns a periodic model with calendar dates, starting positions, or delayed signals.

method: 1. Determine the period first, choose an anchor feature, write B(x-C), and verify at least one additional feature a quarter-period away.
2. Phase shift is defined modulo a full period. Many values of C describe the same function.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: The general sinusoidal function
lessons.outcome: Build and analyze y=A sin(B(x-C))+D and equivalent cosine forms.
opening: A Ferris wheel ranges from 2 to 38 meters, has period 60 seconds, and begins at its lowest point. Write a height model.

lessons.title: Tangent and cotangent graphs
lessons.outcome: Derive tangent and cotangent graphs from quotient definitions, zeros, asymptotes, and period pi.
opening: Sketch tan x on (-pi/2,3pi/2) using sine and cosine signs rather than memory.
Tangent models slopes, perspective, periodic blow-up behavior, and phase response.
exposition: Tangent is sin x/cos x and therefore records the slope of the terminal ray when cosine is nonzero. Cotangent is its reciprocal ratio.
Tangent has zeros where sine is zero, vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero, range all real numbers, and period pi. Each branch increases from negative infinity to positive infinity.
The half-turn period follows because both sine and cosine change sign after pi, leaving their ratio unchanged.

guide.application: Tangent models slopes, perspective, periodic blow-up behavior, and phase response.

method: 1. Mark asymptotes first, place zeros midway between them, use exact values at pi/4 offsets, and apply transformations to the branch structure.
2. A transformed tangent’s vertical shift is a center line, not a horizontal asymptote.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

blocks.text: Sketch tan x on (-pi/2,3pi/2) using sine and cosine signs rather than memory.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.text: Begin by identifying the mathematical object and the information that fixes it. Mark asymptotes first, place zeros midway between them, use exact values at pi/4 offsets, and apply transformations to the branch structure. The relevant conditions are not optional bookkeeping: A transformed tangent’s vertical shift is a center line, not a horizontal asymptote. Following that structure gives Zeros at 0 and pi; asymptotes at -pi/2, pi/2, 3pi/2; increasing branches.

blocks.label: Why this works
blocks.text: The half-turn period follows because both sine and cosine change sign after pi, leaving their ratio unchanged. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.

textbookSections.heading: What this lesson is really about

blocks.text: Tangent is sin x/cos x and therefore records the slope of the terminal ray when cosine is nonzero. Cotangent is its reciprocal ratio.
Tangent has zeros where sine is zero, vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero, range all real numbers, and period pi. Each branch increases from negative infinity to positive infinity.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
The half-turn period follows because both sine and cosine change sign after pi, leaving their ratio unchanged.
Mark asymptotes first, place zeros midway between them, use exact values at pi/4 offsets, and apply transformations to the branch structure.
A transformed tangent’s vertical shift is a center line, not a horizontal asymptote.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is to connect branches across an asymptote or to give tangent the 2pi period of sine.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Secant and cosecant graphs
lessons.outcome: Construct secant and cosecant graphs as reciprocals of cosine and sine.
opening: Use the graph of cos x to sketch sec x on [0,2pi], marking all vertices and asymptotes.
Reciprocal trig graphs appear in optics, wave geometry, and analytic identities.
exposition: Secant and cosecant are the reciprocals of cosine and sine.
Where the parent sine or cosine equals zero, the reciprocal is undefined and has a vertical asymptote. Where the parent reaches 1 or -1, the reciprocal reaches corresponding vertices 1 or -1.
The reciprocal graph cannot cross the interval (-1,1), so its range is (-infinity,-1] union [1,infinity) before transformations.

guide.application: Reciprocal trig graphs appear in optics, wave geometry, and analytic identities.
bigIdea: Secant and cosecant are the reciprocals of cosine and sine.
Where the parent sine or cosine equals zero, the reciprocal is undefined and has a vertical asymptote. Where the parent reaches 1 or -1, the reciprocal reaches corresponding vertices 1 or -1.
method: 1. Graph the underlying sine or cosine lightly, draw asymptotes at its zeros, plot reciprocal vertices at extrema, and sketch branches away from the forbidden band.
2. Transformations change the forbidden band and vertex levels. Solve inequalities carefully to state the range.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Symmetry, periodicity, and the six-function family
lessons.outcome: Compare domains, ranges, parity, periods, zeros, and asymptotes of all six trig functions.
opening: Without graphing, decide which trig functions satisfy f(-x)=-f(x) and which satisfy f(-x)=f(x).
The family comparison is essential for identities and equation solving.
exposition: The six trigonometric functions share a unit-circle origin but differ in domain, range, parity, period, zeros, and asymptotes.
Sine and cosine have period 2pi; tangent and cotangent have period pi; secant and cosecant inherit 2pi. Cosine and secant are even; the other four are odd.
A comparison table makes reciprocal and quotient relationships visible and supports rapid graph identification.

method: 1. Classify a function by its defining ratio, then derive features rather than memorizing six unrelated lists.
2. Transformations can alter visible symmetry about the coordinate axes even though the parent parity remains a reference.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Inverse trigonometric functions and branch restrictions
lessons.outcome: Define inverse sine, cosine, and tangent using one-to-one branches and principal-value ranges.
opening: Why can sin x not have an inverse on all real numbers, and why is [-pi/2,pi/2] a useful restricted domain?
Inverse trig functions recover angles in triangles, equations, vectors, and numerical models.
exposition: Inverse trigonometric functions reverse restricted one-to-one branches of sine, cosine, and tangent.

Arcsine uses sine on [-pi/2,pi/2], arccosine uses cosine on [0,pi], and arctangent uses tangent on (-pi/2,pi/2). These ranges are principal-value conventions chosen to make each restricted function one-to-one while covering its natural range.
The inverse domains are the original ranges: arcsin and arccos accept [-1,1], while arctan accepts all real inputs.

guide.application: Inverse trig functions recover angles in triangles, equations, vectors, and numerical models.

method: 1. Evaluate exact values by finding the principal angle in the required range. For compositions such as sin(arccos u), draw a right triangle or use identities with sign determined by the principal range.

lessons.title: Sinusoidal modeling and regression
lessons.outcome: Fit and critique sinusoidal models using amplitude, midline, period, phase, residuals, and domain.
opening: Monthly daylight hours range from 9.1 to 15.3, with a maximum near day 172. Build a first sinusoidal model with period 365.
Periodic regression supports climate, tides, daylight, acoustics, and mechanical monitoring.
exposition: Sinusoidal modeling estimates a periodic relationship from observed extrema, timing, or regression.
Amplitude, midline, period, and phase carry direct contextual meanings. Regression selects parameters that best fit noisy data but does not prove exact periodicity.

Residuals should be small and patternless if the sinusoidal form captures the main structure. Changing amplitude, drifting midline, multiple frequencies, or irregular timing produce systematic residuals.

blocks.text: Sinusoidal modeling estimates a periodic relationship from observed extrema, timing, or regression.

lessons.title: Identities, equations, and proof strategy
lessons.outcome: Distinguish identities from conditional equations and use valid one-sided transformation strategies.
opening: Is (1-cos^2 x)/sin x=sin x an identity? State the exact common domain on which the equality is valid.
Identity reasoning supports simplification, equation solving, signal analysis, and later calculus manipulations.
exposition: A trigonometric identity is an equation true for every input in the common domain of both sides. A conditional equation is true only for selected inputs.

Identity verification is a proof task: the goal is to transform one expression through valid equivalences until it matches the other. Substituting sample values can detect false statements but cannot prove an identity over infinitely many inputs.
The common domain matters because algebraic simplification can remove a factor that was originally zero or introduce a reciprocal that excludes additional inputs.

lessons.title: Reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean identities
lessons.outcome: Derive and apply the fundamental trig identities from unit-circle coordinates.
opening: Starting from sin^2 x+cos^2 x=1, derive 1+tan^2 x=sec^2 x and state its domain.
The identities provide the algebraic vocabulary for every later trig proof and equation.
exposition: The fundamental identities connect the six trigonometric functions through reciprocal, quotient, and unit-circle relationships.

Reciprocal identities follow from definitions. Quotient identities are tan=sin/cos and cot=cos/sin. The Pythagorean identity sin^2+cos^2=1 comes from the unit circle, and division by cos^2 or sin^2 yields the tangent-secant and cotangent-cosecant forms.
These identities are function equalities on common domains, so division-based versions exclude inputs where the divisor is zero.

textbookSections.heading: What this lesson is really about

blocks.text: The fundamental identities connect the six trigonometric functions through reciprocal, quotient, and unit-circle relationships.

Reciprocal identities follow from definitions. Quotient identities are tan=sin/cos and cot=cos/sin. The Pythagorean identity sin^2+cos^2=1 comes from the unit circle, and division by cos^2 or sin^2 yields the tangent-secant and cotangent-cosecant forms.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
These identities are function equalities on common domains, so division-based versions exclude inputs where the divisor is zero.
When simplifying, choose the identity that replaces the most complicated structure. Converting everything to sine and cosine is reliable but not always shortest.
Squared notation means (sin x)^2, not sin(x^2).

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is to write sin^2 x+cos^2 x as (sin x+cos x)^2 or to omit the cross term when reversing.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Verifying identities strategically
lessons.outcome: Select factoring, common denominators, conjugates, or sine-cosine conversion to verify identities.
opening: Verify (1-cos x)/sin x=sin x/(1+cos x) on the common domain.
Proof strategy trains the same structure recognition used in algebra, calculus, and mathematical writing.
exposition: Strategic identity verification combines trigonometric identities with factoring, common denominators, conjugates, and algebraic simplification.
A proof usually becomes easier when one expression is converted into a common function language or when a denominator is rationalized using a conjugate. The choice depends on visible structure.

Working from the more complicated side avoids replacing a simple target with a larger expression. Sometimes both sides may be transformed independently to the same third expression, but the logic must remain clear.

lessons.title: Half-angle and power-reduction formulas
lessons.outcome: Derive half-angle and power-reduction identities and select signs using quadrant information.
opening: Given cos theta=-5/13 and theta in quadrant III, find sin(theta/2) and cos(theta/2).
Half-angle identities support exact values, equations, and repeated angle subdivision.
exposition: Half-angle formulas recover trig values of x/2 from values at x. Power-reduction formulas rewrite squared trig functions using first powers of cosine at double angle.
Solving the cosine double-angle formulas for sin^2(x/2) and cos^2(x/2) introduces square roots. The sign must be selected from the quadrant containing x/2.
Power reduction is especially useful when squared functions must be compared, averaged, or later integrated.

lessons.outcome: Convert products and sums of trig functions to alternate forms and interpret signal combinations.
opening: Rewrite cos 7x+cos 3x as a product and identify the fast and slow factors.
The formulas explain beats, interference, Fourier-style signal structure, and certain equation transformations.
exposition: Product-to-sum and sum-to-product identities translate between multiplicative and additive combinations of trig functions.
Adding and subtracting angle-sum formulas isolates products such as sin a sin b or cos a cos b. Reversing those identities expresses sums as products involving average and half-difference angles.
The two forms emphasize different structure: sums show component frequencies, while products reveal amplitude envelopes and zeros.

lessons.title: Equations using fundamental identities
lessons.outcome: Solve trig equations by converting functions, factoring, and applying fundamental identities.
opening: Solve sec x=2cos x on [0,2pi).
Identity equations arise in waves, geometry, and transformed periodic models.
exposition: Identity-based trig equations are solved by rewriting all terms into compatible functions and then applying ordinary algebra.
Reciprocal and quotient functions often create domain exclusions. A Pythagorean substitution can reduce an equation to one function before factoring.
The solution process remains two-stage: solve an algebraic condition in function values, then solve the resulting basic trig equations over the required interval or over all reals.

lessons.title: Multiple-angle equations
lessons.outcome: Solve equations involving sin(nx), cos(nx), or tan(nx) and translate solution families back to x.
opening: Solve sin(3x)=sqrt(3)/2 on [0,2pi).
Multiple-angle equations model higher harmonics, repeated rotations, and oscillations with increased frequency.
exposition: A multiple-angle equation treats nx as the temporary angle variable.

Solve the basic equation for the full set of values of nx, then divide every solution family by n. On a restricted x-interval, the corresponding nx-interval is n times as wide and may contain more cycles.
This interval expansion explains why sin(3x)=k can have six solutions on [0,2pi) even though sin u=k has only two per u-period.

lessons.outcome: Use graphing, bracketing, and numerical methods for trig equations without convenient exact solutions.
opening: Solve sin x=0.3x on [0,6] to three decimals.
Numerical trig equations appear in engineering, signal timing, navigation, and nonlinear models.
exposition: Most realistic trigonometric equations require numerical approximation rather than exact unit-circle values.

Graphs locate intersections and estimate root counts. Bracketing methods preserve evidence that a root lies in an interval, while faster iterative methods require good starting values and may converge to unexpected roots.
A numerical answer should include units, angle mode, interval, precision, and a residual or substitution check.

lessons.title: Right triangles and trigonometric ratios
lessons.outcome: Connect unit-circle trig definitions with ratios in similar right triangles.
opening: A ramp rises 0.84 meter over a horizontal run of 7.2 meters. Find its angle of inclination and length.

exposition: Right-triangle trigonometry expresses side ratios as functions of an acute angle.

All right triangles sharing an acute angle are similar, so opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse, and opposite/adjacent ratios remain constant. These ratios agree with unit-circle sine, cosine, and tangent in the first quadrant.
A triangle problem is determined by enough independent side and angle information, together with the right angle.

lessons.title: Right-triangle applications
lessons.outcome: Model heights, distances, slopes, and angles of elevation or depression.
opening: From a point 80 meters from a building, the angle of elevation to the roof is 37 degrees. The instrument is 1.6 meters high. Find building height.
Applications include surveying, ramps, astronomy, construction, and navigation.
exposition: Right-triangle applications convert a physical situation into a geometric model before any trigonometric calculation.
Angles of elevation and depression are measured from horizontal lines. Parallel horizontals often create equal alternate interior angles, but the diagram must show why.
Instrument height, ground slope, observer position, and line of sight may create offsets that must be added after the triangle calculation.

lessons.title: The Law of Sines
lessons.outcome: Derive and apply the Law of Sines to ASA, AAS, and suitable SSA triangles.
opening: A triangle has A=42 degrees, B=71 degrees, and side a=18. Find sides b and c.
The Law of Sines supports triangulation, navigation, astronomy, and surveying.
exposition: The Law of Sines states that side lengths are proportional to the sines of their opposite angles.
An altitude derivation shows that different expressions for the same height lead to a/sin A=b/sin B. The common value also equals the circumcircle diameter 2R.
The law is most direct for ASA and AAS data because the third angle is known and an opposite pair is available. SSA requires a separate ambiguity analysis.

lessons.title: The Law of Cosines
lessons.outcome: Use the Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS data and connect it to the Pythagorean theorem.
opening: Two sides of a triangle are 11 and 16 with included angle 124 degrees. Find the third side.
The law supports distance, structural geometry, navigation, and vector magnitude calculations.
exposition: The Law of Cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to any triangle.
In c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab cos C, the correction term accounts for the included angle. At C=90 degrees, cosine is zero and the Pythagorean theorem returns.
SAS data determine the opposite side; SSS data determine angles. For SSS, finding the largest angle first provides a useful validity and rounding check.

2. When solving for an angle, the computed cosine must lie in [-1,1]. Rounding intermediate side values may distort later angles.

lessons.title: Triangle area formulas
lessons.outcome: Use K=(1/2)ab sin C and compare with base-height and Heron forms.
opening: Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 and 14 enclosing 52 degrees.
Triangle area supports surveying, design, force geometry, and coordinate calculations.
exposition: The area formula K=(1/2)ab sin C uses two sides and their included angle.
Dropping an altitude gives height b sin C, so ordinary one-half base times height becomes the sine-area formula. Heron’s formula uses all three sides through the semiperimeter.
The sine formula reveals that two different included angles with the same sine can produce the same area, subject to triangle validity.

lessons.title: Bearings and navigation
lessons.outcome: Translate among standard angles, quadrant bearings, headings, and triangle or component models.
opening: A boat travels 18 km on bearing N35E, then 25 km on bearing S70E. Find its displacement magnitude and bearing.
Bearings support aviation, maritime navigation, surveying, and search planning.
exposition: Bearings encode direction relative to north-south or as clockwise headings from north, while standard mathematical angles begin east and increase counterclockwise.
A navigation path can be solved with triangle laws or vector components. Components are often more reliable for several legs because they preserve signed east-west and north-south contributions.
Quadrant bearings such as N35E specify an acute angle measured from a named north-south ray toward east or west.

guide.application: Bearings support aviation, maritime navigation, surveying, and search planning.
bigIdea: Bearings encode direction relative to north-south or as clockwise headings from north, while standard mathematical angles begin east and increase counterclockwise.

lessons.title: Vectors geometrically and in components
lessons.outcome: Represent vectors by magnitude and direction, add them geometrically, and convert to components.
opening: A force of 80 N acts at 135 degrees. Write its component vector.
Vectors model displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and data transformations.
exposition: A vector has magnitude and direction but no fixed location. Component form records horizontal and vertical contributions.
Vector addition combines displacements or effects. The head-to-tail and parallelogram constructions are geometric versions of componentwise addition.
A vector of magnitude M at standard angle theta has components <M cos theta,M sin theta>. Recover magnitude with the distance formula and direction with quadrant-aware inverse tangent.

lessons.title: Dot product, angles, and projection
lessons.outcome: Use the dot product to find angles, test orthogonality, and calculate projections.
opening: Find the angle between u=<2,5> and v=<4,-1>.
Dot products model work, lighting, similarity, orthogonality, and directional influence.
exposition: The dot product u·v equals the sum of component products and also equals ||u||||v||cos theta.
The two forms connect algebra with geometry. A positive dot product indicates an acute angle, zero indicates perpendicular vectors, and a negative value indicates an obtuse angle.
Projection measures the part of one vector aligned with another. The scalar projection is u·v/||v||, and the vector projection is (u·v/||v||^2)v.

lessons.title: Conics as loci and the circle foundation
lessons.outcome: Define loci by distance conditions and derive the standard circle equation.
opening: Find the locus of points exactly 5 units from (-2,3) and determine its x- and y-intercepts.
Circle loci support navigation, coverage, orbits, construction, and the geometric origin of trigonometry.
exposition: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a geometric condition. A circle is the locus of points at a fixed distance r from a center (h,k).

Applying the distance formula and squaring gives (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2. The equation is usually an implicit relation rather than one function y=f(x), because most x-values inside the circle correspond to two y-values.
Completing squares converts general quadratic expressions into center-radius form and reveals whether the relation is a circle, a point, or an empty set.

method: 1. Identify the distance condition, write the equation before expanding, and use systems with x=0 or y=0 to find intercepts.
2. The radius must be nonnegative. A negative squared-radius value produces no real points, while radius zero produces one point.

lessons.title: Parabolas from focus and directrix
lessons.outcome: Derive and analyze parabolas as points equidistant from a focus and directrix.
opening: Find the equation of points equidistant from focus (0,3) and directrix y=-3.
Parabolic reflection explains satellite dishes, headlights, microphones, and projectile approximations.
exposition: A parabola is the locus of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix.

Equating point-to-focus distance with perpendicular distance to the directrix and simplifying produces (x-h)^2=4p(y-k) or (y-k)^2=4p(x-h). The parameter p is the directed distance from the vertex to the focus.
The sign of p determines opening direction. The focus and directrix are equally distant from the vertex on opposite sides.

guide.application: Parabolic reflection explains satellite dishes, headlights, microphones, and projectile approximations.

method: 1. Identify orientation, place the vertex halfway between focus and directrix, write the standard form, and verify one point using the distance condition.

lessons.title: Ellipses
lessons.outcome: Analyze ellipses from constant-sum distance and standard equations.
opening: An ellipse has foci (-4,0),(4,0) and constant distance sum 10. Find its standard equation.
Ellipses model orbits, acoustics, architecture, and constant-total-distance constraints.
exposition: An ellipse is the locus of points whose distances to two foci have a constant sum 2a.
In standard form, a is the semimajor axis, b the semiminor axis, and c the center-to-focus distance, with c^2=a^2-b^2. The larger denominator identifies the major-axis direction.
The circle is the special case c=0 and a=b. As c approaches a, the ellipse becomes more elongated.

In standard form, a is the semimajor axis, b the semiminor axis, and c the center-to-focus distance, with c^2=a^2-b^2. The larger denominator identifies the major-axis direction.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
The circle is the special case c=0 and a=b. As c approaches a, the ellipse becomes more elongated.
Read center and denominators, determine orientation, calculate c, and list vertices, covertices, foci, and axis lengths.
The standard equation assumes positive denominators and right side 1. Translated forms require center shifts before features are read.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is placing the foci using b instead of c or assuming the larger denominator always belongs under x.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Hyperbolas
lessons.outcome: Analyze hyperbolas from constant-difference distance and standard equations.
opening: A hyperbola has center (0,0), vertices (±3,0), and foci (±5,0). Find its equation and asymptotes.
Hyperbolas appear in navigation differences, cooling-tower sections, optics, and inverse-product graphs after transformation.
exposition: A hyperbola is the locus of points whose absolute difference of distances to two foci is constant 2a.
Its standard forms contain one positive squared term and one negative squared term. The positive term identifies the transverse-axis direction. The focal relationship is c^2=a^2+b^2.
Asymptotes pass through the center and follow the diagonals of the fundamental rectangle with semiaxes a and b.

method: 1. Determine center and orientation, locate vertices, compute c, draw the fundamental rectangle, and sketch branches approaching the asymptotes.
2. The two branches are separate components of one relation. The asymptotes guide end behavior but are not part of the hyperbola.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Completing squares in two variables
lessons.outcome: Convert general quadratic relations to standard conic form by completing squares.
opening: Classify and graph x^2+6x+4y^2-8y=11.
The technique connects general quadratic equations to geometric conic parameters.
exposition: Completing the square rewrites quadratic expressions so translated centers, vertices, and axes become visible.
For x^2+Bx, add (B/2)^2 inside a balanced equation. When a coefficient multiplies x^2 or y^2, factor it from the entire variable group before completing the square.
Both variable groups and the equation’s right side must remain balanced. The final constant determines scale and may reveal a degenerate or empty relation.

guide.application: The technique connects general quadratic equations to geometric conic parameters.
bigIdea: Completing the square rewrites quadratic expressions so translated centers, vertices, and axes become visible.
For x^2+Bx, add (B/2)^2 inside a balanced equation. When a coefficient multiplies x^2 or y^2, factor it from the entire variable group before completing the square.
method: 1. Collect x and y terms, move constants, factor leading coefficients, complete each square, combine constants, and normalize the right side when needed.
2. If a squared coefficient is negative, factoring changes the sign of the completion constant and must be tracked carefully.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Translated conics and general equations
lessons.outcome: Classify translated conics and recover all geometric features from standard form.
opening: Classify 9x^2+4y^2-54x+16y+61=0 and find center, axes, and vertices.
General equations arise from algebraic models, intersections, and coordinate changes.
exposition: A translated conic equation can be classified from the signs and relative coefficients of its squared terms after rotation-free standardization.
Same-sign equal coefficients suggest a circle, same-sign unequal coefficients an ellipse, one squared variable a parabola, and opposite signs a hyperbola, subject to degeneracy.
Completing squares provides center or vertex translations. Dividing by the final constant normalizes the equation to standard form.

lessons.title: Degenerate conics and classification
lessons.outcome: Identify point, line, pair-of-lines, empty-set, and other degenerate quadratic relations.
opening: Describe the graph of x^2+y^2+4x-6y+13=0.
Degenerate cases matter in parameter families, optimization boundaries, and algebraic classification.
exposition: A degenerate conic occurs when the usual conic equation collapses into a point, line, pair of lines, or empty set.
Factorization and completed-square form reveal these cases. For example, x^2-y^2=0 factors into (x-y)(x+y)=0, the union of two lines.

lessons.title: Eccentricity and unified conic structure
lessons.outcome: Use eccentricity to compare circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.
opening: A conic has focus at (4,0), directrix x=9, and eccentricity 1/2. Determine its type and derive an equation.
Eccentricity describes orbital shape, optical design, and a unified family of conics.
exposition: Eccentricity e compares a point’s distance to a focus with its distance to a directrix.
The ratio distinguishes conic families: 0<e<1 gives an ellipse, e=1 a parabola, and e>1 a hyperbola. A circle is the limiting symmetric case e=0.
For standard ellipses and hyperbolas, e=c/a. Increasing e stretches an ellipse toward a parabola and opens a hyperbola more strongly relative to its vertex distance.

opening: A satellite dish is 3.6 meters wide and 0.45 meter deep. Find focal distance.

exposition: Conic models use geometric parameters to represent reflectors, orbits, acoustic paths, arches, and cross-sections.
A parabolic reflector’s focal distance follows from width and depth. Ellipse foci explain whispering-gallery paths, and hyperbolic differences support navigation methods.
Real structures approximate ideal conics over selected regions. Materials, loading, thickness, measurement error, and three-dimensional effects limit the model.

lessons.title: Parametric equations and orientation
lessons.outcome: Interpret x=f(t), y=g(t) as a directed path with a parameter interval.
opening: For x=2t-1 and y=t^2, -2≤t≤3, find endpoints, direction, and the Cartesian curve.
Parametric equations model motion, closed curves, projectiles, mechanical linkages, and paths that fail the vertical-line test.
exposition: Parametric equations describe x and y as coordinated functions of a third variable t.
The parameter determines not only the geometric path but also starting point, direction, timing, and repeated traversal. Two parametrizations can trace the same set of points differently.
A table of t-values reveals ordered positions. Arrows on the curve preserve orientation information that is absent from an ordinary Cartesian equation.

lessons.outcome: Eliminate parameters while preserving interval restrictions and lost orientation information.
opening: Eliminate t from x=t+1, y=t^2-4 for -2≤t≤3.

exposition: Eliminating a parameter produces a Cartesian relation containing the parametric path.

lessons.title: Parametric motion and vector-valued position
lessons.outcome: Use r(t)=<x(t),y(t)> to describe position, displacement, and average velocity.
opening: A particle has r(t)=<t^2-1,3t>. Find displacement and average velocity from t=1 to t=4.
Vector-valued motion supports navigation, robotics, projectiles, and the later calculus of parametric curves.
exposition: A vector-valued position function r(t)=<x(t),y(t)> records planar motion.
Displacement over [a,b] is r(b)-r(a), while average velocity is displacement divided by b-a. These quantities differ from path length and average speed.
Component changes can be interpreted separately, but the vector preserves direction and combined magnitude.

method: 1. Evaluate endpoint positions, subtract componentwise, divide by elapsed time, and attach units.

lessons.title: Polar coordinates and nonuniqueness
lessons.outcome: Represent points as (r,theta), use negative radius, and generate equivalent polar coordinates.
opening: Plot (-4,5pi/6) and give two equivalent representations with positive radius.
Polar coordinates naturally describe rotation, radial symmetry, spirals, roses, and conics with a focus at the pole.
exposition: A polar coordinate pair (r,theta) locates a point by signed distance from the pole and direction from the polar axis.
Positive r moves along the ray theta; negative r moves |r| units along the opposite ray. Adding 2pi k to theta gives equivalent coordinates, and changing the sign of r can be offset by adding pi.
Polar coordinates are therefore nonunique. The same point has infinitely many representations.

2. The pole r=0 has every angle representation, so its angle is indeterminate.
