textbookSections.heading: What this lesson is really about

blocks.text: A polar coordinate pair (r,theta) locates a point by signed distance from the pole and direction from the polar axis.
Positive r moves along the ray theta; negative r moves |r| units along the opposite ray. Adding 2pi k to theta gives equivalent coordinates, and changing the sign of r can be offset by adding pi.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
Polar coordinates are therefore nonunique. The same point has infinitely many representations.
Draw the direction ray, apply the sign of r, and generate equivalent forms systematically rather than by visual guess.
The pole r=0 has every angle representation, so its angle is indeterminate.

A common error is plotting negative radius on the same ray instead of the opposite ray.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

opening: Convert the line x=4 to a polar equation and state where the formula is undefined.

exposition: Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by x=r cos theta, y=r sin theta, r^2=x^2+y^2, and tan theta=y/x with quadrant care.

lessons.outcome: Trace r=f(theta) using tables, signed radius, and interval selection.
opening: Trace r=2+2cos theta over 0≤theta≤2pi and identify intercepts and maximum radius.
Polar tracing represents antennas, orbital shapes, petals, spirals, and directional measurements.
exposition: A polar graph r=f(theta) assigns a signed radius to each direction input.
As theta changes, both the ray and radius change. Negative radii reverse the plotted direction, so a simple table must include sign interpretation rather than only numerical magnitude.
Key angles, zeros, maxima, minima, and symmetry provide the skeleton of the curve. Arrows indicate tracing order.

lessons.title: Polar symmetry and repeated tracing
lessons.outcome: Test symmetry and choose intervals that trace a polar curve exactly once.
opening: Determine all standard polar symmetries of r=2cos(3theta) and an interval that traces it once.
Symmetry reduces graphing work and reveals parameter structure.
exposition: Polar symmetry can be tested by substitutions that leave an equivalent equation.

Replacing theta with -theta tests symmetry about the polar axis; replacing theta with pi-theta tests symmetry about the vertical line; replacing r with -r or theta with theta+pi tests symmetry about the pole.
Because polar representations are nonunique, an equation can be symmetric even when a substituted form does not simplify literally to the original.

lessons.title: Complex numbers in polar form
lessons.outcome: Represent complex numbers by modulus and argument and convert between rectangular and polar forms.
opening: Write z=-3+3sqrt(3)i in polar form using a principal argument.
Polar complex form connects algebra with rotations and scaling.
exposition: A nonzero complex number z=a+bi can be represented by modulus r=sqrt(a^2+b^2) and argument theta, giving z=r(cos theta+i sin theta).
This is the polar coordinate representation of the point (a,b) in the complex plane. The argument is nonunique modulo 2pi; a principal argument is chosen from a stated interval.
Rectangular form is best for addition, while polar form reveals multiplication, division, powers, and roots.

guide.application: Polar complex form connects algebra with rotations and scaling.
bigIdea: A nonzero complex number z=a+bi can be represented by modulus r=sqrt(a^2+b^2) and argument theta, giving z=r(cos theta+i sin theta).

method: 1. Compute the modulus, choose a quadrant-correct argument, and verify by converting back with cosine and sine.
2. The zero complex number has modulus zero but no unique argument.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

blocks.label: Worked development
blocks.text: Compute the modulus, choose a quadrant-correct argument, and verify by converting back with cosine and sine. In this example, the first useful move is to make the defining structure visible rather than to search for a memorized answer. This is the polar coordinate representation of the point (a,b) in the complex plane. The argument is nonunique modulo 2pi; a principal argument is chosen from a stated interval. Then apply the conditions explicitly: The zero complex number has modulus zero but no unique argument. Finish by checking the result in a second representation and explaining what the result means.

lessons.title: Roots of complex numbers
lessons.outcome: Find all nth roots of a complex number and interpret their equal angular spacing.
opening: Find all cube roots of 8i.
Complex roots complete polynomial solution sets and create regular polygons in the complex plane.
exposition: The nth roots of a nonzero complex number are equally spaced around a circle.
If w=R cis phi, then each root has modulus R^{1/n} and argument (phi+2pi k)/n for k=0,...,n-1. Adding n to k repeats the first root.
The 2pi k term is essential because the same target number has infinitely many arguments before division by n.

2. The zero number has one nth root, zero, rather than n distinct roots.

If w=R cis phi, then each root has modulus R^{1/n} and argument (phi+2pi k)/n for k=0,...,n-1. Adding n to k repeats the first root.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
The 2pi k term is essential because the same target number has infinitely many arguments before division by n.
Write the target in polar form, apply the root formula, list exactly n distinct roots, and verify by raising one or all roots to the nth power.
The zero number has one nth root, zero, rather than n distinct roots.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is using only the principal argument and finding one root.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

blocks.text: Find all cube roots of 8i.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.text: Begin by identifying the mathematical object and the information that fixes it. Following that structure gives 8i=8cis(pi/2); roots have modulus 2 and arguments pi/6+2kpi/3 for k=0,1,2.

lessons.title: Sequences as discrete functions
lessons.outcome: Interpret a sequence as a function on an integer index set.
opening: The first five terms are 4,7,12,19,28. Plot them as a discrete function and propose a formula.
Sequences model samples, payments, populations, algorithms, and repeated experiments.
exposition: A sequence is a function whose domain is an ordered discrete index set, commonly the positive or nonnegative integers.
The index n identifies position; a_n is the term value. A sequence graph consists of isolated points because intermediate indices are not part of the domain unless separately defined.
A formula, table, recurrence, graph, or verbal process may describe the same sequence.

lessons.title: Explicit and recursive descriptions
lessons.outcome: Move among term lists, explicit formulas, recursive rules, tables, and plots.
opening: A sequence begins 3,8,18,38,78. Write a recurrence and an explicit formula.
Explicit-recursive translation supports algorithms, finance, population models, and discrete dynamics.
exposition: An explicit rule computes a_n directly from n, while a recursive rule computes a term from earlier terms and initial conditions.
Recursion mirrors repeated processes and can describe patterns without a simple closed form. Explicit rules make distant terms easier to evaluate.
An initial condition is essential because the same recurrence can generate infinitely many sequences from different starting values.

lessons.outcome: Analyze repeated function application, fixed points, cycles, and qualitative long-run behavior.
opening: A population follows P_{n+1}=0.6P_n+80 with P_0=50. Compute six terms and predict the limiting value.
Discrete dynamics model populations, loans, feedback, algorithms, and control systems.
exposition: A recurrence x_{n+1}=f(x_n) repeatedly applies one function to the current state.
A fixed point L satisfies L=f(L). Whether nearby terms approach or move away from L depends on how the iteration changes deviations, a concept explored qualitatively here.
Some recurrences converge, diverge, oscillate, or enter cycles. The term graph and a cobweb diagram reveal different aspects of the process.

opening: Expand and evaluate sum from k=2 to 6 of (3k-1).

lessons.title: Arithmetic series
lessons.outcome: Derive and use S_n=n(a_1+a_n)/2.
opening: Find the total number of seats in 35 auditorium rows when the first has 18 and each adds 4.
Arithmetic sums model total seating, regular payments, stacked objects, and cumulative linear change.
exposition: An arithmetic series is the finite sum of an arithmetic sequence.
Writing the sum forward and backward pairs the first and last terms, the second and next-to-last, and so on. Every pair has sum a_1+a_n, producing S_n=n(a_1+a_n)/2.
The formula is also n times the average of the endpoints, which matches the average value of a linear sequence.

guide.application: Arithmetic sums model total seating, regular payments, stacked objects, and cumulative linear change.

method: 1. Find a_n if necessary, identify the number of terms from indexing, apply the formula, and attach units.
2. When n is odd, the middle term pairs with itself conceptually; the formula remains valid.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Infinite geometric series and convergence
lessons.outcome: Determine convergence and evaluate infinite geometric sums when |r|<1.
opening: A ball is dropped from 12 meters and rebounds to 3/4 of each previous height. Find its total vertical travel.
Infinite geometric series model recurring decimals, rebounds, annuities, and self-similar constructions.
exposition: An infinite series is defined through the limit of its sequence of partial sums.
For a geometric series, r^n approaches zero exactly when |r|<1, so the partial sums approach a/(1-r). If |r|≥1, the terms fail to shrink appropriately or the partial sums diverge.

The term sequence and partial-sum sequence are different objects. Terms may approach zero without guaranteeing convergence for a general series, though the geometric case is completely classified by r.

method: 1. Identify a and r, test |r|<1 before using the formula, and distinguish total path length from signed displacement in applications.
2. Negative r can produce oscillatory convergence. The sum may lie between successive partial sums.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

opening: Induction proves sum formulas, divisibility, inequalities, and recursive identities.

lessons.title: Pascal's triangle and binomial coefficients
lessons.outcome: Connect combinations, recursive construction, symmetry, and polynomial coefficients.
opening: Find the coefficient of x^4 in (2+x)^7 without expanding the whole polynomial.
Binomial coefficients connect algebra, probability, combinatorics, and discrete models.
exposition: Pascal’s triangle organizes binomial coefficients, with each interior entry equal to the sum of the two entries above it.
The entry C(n,k) counts selections of k objects from n and also appears as the coefficient of a^{n-k}b^k in (a+b)^n.
Symmetry C(n,k)=C(n,n-k) follows from choosing a subset or choosing its complement.

lessons.title: The binomial theorem and discrete-model synthesis
lessons.outcome: Expand binomial powers and compare arithmetic, geometric, recursive, and accumulated models.
opening: Find the first four nonzero terms of (1-2x)^8.
The binomial theorem supports probability, approximation, combinatorial identities, and polynomial structure.
exposition: The binomial theorem expands (a+b)^n as a sum of terms C(n,k)a^{n-k}b^k.
As k increases, the exponent of a decreases while the exponent of b increases, and the total degree remains n. Signs alternate automatically when b is negative.
A specified term can be found directly without expanding the entire polynomial.

lessons.title: Function-family classification
lessons.outcome: Classify unfamiliar formulas, graphs, tables, and contexts using structural evidence.
opening: A graph is positive, decreasing, concave upward, has domain all reals, and approaches y=2 as x grows. Name plausible families and identify one additional feature needed.
Family recognition is the organizing skill behind all of Precalculus and the first step in many Calculus problems.
exposition: Function-family classification uses domain, range, transformations, rate patterns, zeros, asymptotes, periodicity, and representation type as evidence.
No single visual feature is always decisive. Several families can share a point, slope, or short-term shape. Strong classification eliminates alternatives by structural invariants.
A formula may combine families, and a graph may be piecewise, parametric, polar, or discrete rather than one ordinary elementary function.

method: 1. Inventory domain and restrictions, inspect differences or ratios, identify symmetry and end behavior, and state both the best candidate and the evidence still needed.
2. Classification is a model-selection claim, not a demand that every data set belong perfectly to one named family.

lessons.title: Model selection and comparison
lessons.outcome: Select and compare function models using patterns, residuals, domains, and parameter meanings.
opening: Three models fit the same ten data points: linear, exponential, and logistic. What evidence should decide among them?
Model comparison supports scientific reasoning, economics, engineering, and data analysis.
exposition: Model selection compares how well different function families explain data, structure, and context.
Residual size matters, but so do residual pattern, parameter meaning, domain behavior, long-run prediction, simplicity, and mechanism.
Two models can fit the observed interval similarly while producing radically different extrapolations.

guide.application: Model comparison supports scientific reasoning, economics, engineering, and data analysis.

2. A more complicated model can overfit noise. A simpler model can miss real structure.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Difference quotients
lessons.outcome: Construct and simplify [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h and interpret its components.
opening: Simplify the difference quotient for f(x)=x^2-3x.
Difference quotients are the algebraic raw material of derivatives.
exposition: The difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h is the average rate of change over an interval of width h beginning at x.
Algebraic simplification often cancels h, revealing how the secant slope depends on x and interval width. The original quotient still requires h≠0.
Polynomial quotients use expansion and factoring; rational quotients use common denominators; radical quotients often use conjugates.

guide.application: Difference quotients are the algebraic raw material of derivatives.
bigIdea: The difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h is the average rate of change over an interval of width h beginning at x.
Algebraic simplification often cancels h, revealing how the secant slope depends on x and interval width. The original quotient still requires h≠0.
method: 1. Write f(x+h) with full grouping, subtract the entire f(x), factor or rationalize, cancel only common factors, and retain h≠0.
2. Cancellation creates a simplified formula for nonzero h; it does not define the original secant at h=0.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.
questions: Which definition or geometric structure controls difference quotients?

blocks.text: Simplify the difference quotient for f(x)=x^2-3x.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.text: Begin by identifying the mathematical object and the information that fixes it. Write f(x+h) with full grouping, subtract the entire f(x), factor or rationalize, cancel only common factors, and retain h≠0. The relevant conditions are not optional bookkeeping: Cancellation creates a simplified formula for nonzero h; it does not define the original secant at h=0. Following that structure gives 2x+h-3, for h≠0.

blocks.label: Why this works
blocks.text: Polynomial quotients use expansion and factoring; rational quotients use common denominators; radical quotients often use conjugates. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.

textbookSections.heading: What this lesson is really about

blocks.text: The difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h is the average rate of change over an interval of width h beginning at x.
Algebraic simplification often cancels h, revealing how the secant slope depends on x and interval width. The original quotient still requires h≠0.

lessons.title: Secant lines and tangent intuition
lessons.outcome: Interpret tangent slope as a limiting value of secant slopes.
opening: For f(x)=x^2 at x=2, calculate secant slopes using h=1,0.5,0.1,0.01 and predict the tangent slope.
Secant-to-tangent reasoning motivates derivatives, velocity, and local approximation.
exposition: A secant line passes through two graph points; a tangent line describes local direction at one point.
As the second point approaches the first, secant slopes may approach a limiting value. That value becomes the tangent slope in Calculus.
Left and right approaches can disagree at corners, while slopes can grow without bound near vertical tangents.

lessons.title: Local linearity and magnification
lessons.outcome: Recognize when a smooth graph appears linear under magnification and identify failures of local linearity.
opening: Zoom around x=1 on y=x^2 and build the tangent-line approximation from the predicted slope 2.
Local linearity supports estimation, measurement error analysis, and the conceptual meaning of derivatives.
exposition: Local linearity is the tendency of a smooth function to resemble its tangent line over a sufficiently small interval.
A linear approximation uses a known value and local slope: L(x)=f(a)+m(x-a). The approximation error usually shrinks as x moves closer to a for differentiable functions.
Corners, cusps, discontinuities, and violent oscillation can defeat a single local line.

2. A graph appearing linear at one screen resolution is visual evidence, not a proof of differentiability.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

lessons.title: Intuitive limits
lessons.outcome: Estimate limits from tables, graphs, and algebra while distinguishing approached value from function value.
opening: Evaluate the limiting value of (x^2-1)/(x-1) as x approaches 1, and compare with the function value at 1.
Limits organize continuity, derivatives, asymptotes, and infinite processes.
exposition: A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input approaches a target, regardless of whether the function equals that value at the target.
Graphs, tables, and algebra provide complementary evidence. One-sided limits must agree for a finite two-sided limit to exist.
Factoring and cancellation can reveal the behavior near a removable hole, while conjugates or common denominators can remove other indeterminate forms.

lessons.title: Continuity and discontinuity
lessons.outcome: Classify removable, jump, infinite, and endpoint discontinuities using function values and limiting behavior.
opening: Choose k so that f(x)=(x^2-4)/(x-2) for x≠2 and f(2)=k is continuous.
Continuity supports existence arguments, model reliability, and later theorems of Calculus.
exposition: A function is continuous at an interior point c when f(c) exists, the two-sided limit exists, and the limit equals f(c).
Removable discontinuities have a common approached value but a missing or incorrect point. Jump discontinuities have unequal one-sided limits. Infinite discontinuities involve unbounded behavior.
At domain endpoints, one-sided continuity is the relevant concept.

guide.application: Continuity supports existence arguments, model reliability, and later theorems of Calculus.
bigIdea: A function is continuous at an interior point c when f(c) exists, the two-sided limit exists, and the limit equals f(c).
Removable discontinuities have a common approached value but a missing or incorrect point. Jump discontinuities have unequal one-sided limits. Infinite discontinuities involve unbounded behavior.
method: 1. Check the function value, left limit, and right limit separately, then classify the first failed condition and determine whether a redefinition can repair it.
2. Continuity depends on the declared domain. A function can be continuous everywhere in its domain while having excluded endpoints or asymptotes outside that domain.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.
questions: Which definition or geometric structure controls continuity and discontinuity?
Which conditions or branch restrictions must remain visible?

lessons.title: Infinite behavior and asymptotes
lessons.outcome: Synthesize finite and infinite input behavior across polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric families.
opening: Compare x^3, 2^x, ln x, and sin x as x approaches infinity.
Infinite behavior prepares students for limits, improper processes, and asymptotic model comparison.
exposition: Infinite behavior distinguishes large input from large output and separates divergence, asymptotic approach, and oscillation.

Polynomial powers, exponentials, logarithms, rationals, and trig functions exhibit different growth and limiting patterns. A function can fail to have a limit while remaining bounded, as sine does at infinity.
Vertical asymptotes concern input approaching a finite excluded value; horizontal or polynomial asymptotes concern large input behavior.

guide.application: Infinite behavior prepares students for limits, improper processes, and asymptotic model comparison.
bigIdea: Infinite behavior distinguishes large input from large output and separates divergence, asymptotic approach, and oscillation.

Polynomial powers, exponentials, logarithms, rationals, and trig functions exhibit different growth and limiting patterns. A function can fail to have a limit while remaining bounded, as sine does at infinity.
method: 1. State the input direction and output behavior explicitly, compare leading structures, and avoid using the infinity symbol as though it were an ordinary number.
2. Growth-rate comparisons depend on the direction and domain. Exponential growth eventually dominates polynomial growth for positive large input.
3. Verify the result in a second representation and explain what it means in the original setting.

opening: A pump's rate is 4,6,9,7 liters per minute over four one-minute intervals. Estimate total volume added using left-endpoint rectangles.

textbookSections.heading: The problem that opens the lesson

blocks.text: A pump's rate is 4,6,9,7 liters per minute over four one-minute intervals. Estimate total volume added using left-endpoint rectangles.

blocks.label: Solution
blocks.text: Begin by identifying the mathematical object and the information that fixes it. Choose left, right, or midpoint sample values, multiply each by interval width, sum with units, and state whether the result is signed net change or total accumulation. The relevant conditions are not optional bookkeeping: A graph’s geometric area and a signed accumulation differ below the input axis. Following that structure gives 4+6+9+7=26 liters.

blocks.label: Why this works
blocks.text: Narrower intervals can improve an estimate when the rate varies, motivating the limiting process behind the definite integral. The calculation and the representation should agree, so a graph, diagram, table, or substitution check should support the same conclusion.

textbookSections.heading: What this lesson is really about

blocks.text: Accumulation combines many local contributions into a total. When a rate is approximately constant over short intervals, rate times interval width estimates the contribution.
Adding rectangle areas under a rate graph produces a finite sum. Positive and negative rates contribute signed net change, while total distance or total amount may require absolute values.

The point is not merely to reproduce a formula. A learner should be able to identify the quantities or geometric objects involved, explain why the relationship has its stated form, and recognize when the same idea appears in a graph, table, diagram, or model.
Narrower intervals can improve an estimate when the rate varies, motivating the limiting process behind the definite integral.
Choose left, right, or midpoint sample values, multiply each by interval width, sum with units, and state whether the result is signed net change or total accumulation.
A graph’s geometric area and a signed accumulation differ below the input axis.

After the symbolic work is complete, check the result. Depending on the lesson, this may mean substituting into an original equation, comparing coordinates, examining a graph, checking units, testing an interval, or confirming that every branch of a periodic solution has been included.
A common error is adding rate values without multiplying by time or another input width.

The repair is to return to the definition and identify the first step where the invalid solution stops describing the original mathematical object. Later algebra cannot rescue a first step that changed the domain, orientation, branch, or meaning of the problem.

lessons.title: Precalculus synthesis capstone

The capstone demonstrates readiness to enter Calculus as a connected study of change and accumulation rather than a collection of new formulas.

routes.title: Precalculus: Functions, Models, and Change
routes.description: A continuous Precalculus course built around functions, multiple representations, exact reasoning, modeling, and change.

routes.title: Algebra and Function Readiness
routes.description: A readiness diagnostic separates prerequisite strands so that a learner receives targeted repair rather than one vague total score.

routes.title: Functions and Multiple Representations
routes.description: An input is supplied to a relationship, an output is determined by it, and parameters remain fixed for one selected model.

routes.title: Transformations and Function Operations
routes.description: A parent function is a convenient reference member identified by domain, range, symmetry, endpoints, asymptotes, and rate patterns.

routes.title: Composition, Inverses, and Modeling
routes.description: Composition represents an ordered chain in which the inner function acts first.

routes.title: Polynomial Functions
routes.description: Power functions f(x)=ax^p connect positive, negative, and fractional exponent behavior.

routes.title: Rational Functions
routes.description: A rational function P/Q excludes every real input where the original denominator Q is zero.

routes.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
routes.description: Constant first differences indicate additive linear change; constant ratios indicate multiplicative exponential change.

routes.title: Systems, Matrices, and Multivariable Models
routes.description: A system solution satisfies every equation simultaneously and appears graphically as a common intersection.

routes.title: Angles, Radians, and the Unit Circle
routes.description: A radar arm begins on the positive x-axis, rotates 765 degrees counterclockwise, then 180 degrees clockwise. Where is its terminal side, and what is the smallest positive coterminal angle?

routes.title: Trigonometric Functions and Periodic Models
routes.description: A point starts at (1,0) and rotates counterclockwise one revolution in 8 seconds. Sketch its vertical coordinate against time and label zeros, extrema, and period.

routes.title: Trigonometric Identities and Equations
routes.description: Is (1-cos^2 x)/sin x=sin x an identity? State the exact common domain on which the equality is valid.

routes.title: Triangle Trigonometry and Vectors
routes.description: A ramp rises 0.84 meter over a horizontal run of 7.2 meters. Find its angle of inclination and length.

routes.title: Conic Sections and Implicit Relations
routes.description: Find the locus of points exactly 5 units from (-2,3) and determine its x- and y-intercepts.

routes.title: Parametric, Polar, and Complex Representations
routes.description: For x=2t-1 and y=t^2, -2≤t≤3, find endpoints, direction, and the Cartesian curve.

routes.title: Sequences, Series, and Discrete Models
routes.description: The first five terms are 4,7,12,19,28. Plot them as a discrete function and propose a formula.

routes.title: Calculus Readiness and Function Synthesis
routes.description: A graph is positive, decreasing, concave upward, has domain all reals, and approaches y=2 as x grows. Name plausible families and identify one additional feature needed.

routes.title: Readiness diagnostic and routing
routes.description: Use diagnostic evidence to identify which prerequisite strands are secure and which require targeted repair.

routes.title: Equation and inequality repair
routes.description: Classify and solve common equation and inequality families while distinguishing reversible steps from candidate-generating steps.

routes.title: Factoring and polynomial structure repair
routes.description: Recognize and apply the principal factoring structures needed for polynomial-function analysis.

routes.title: Rational expressions and restrictions repair
routes.description: Simplify and solve rational expressions while preserving every restriction from the original form.

routes.title: Radicals and rational exponents repair
routes.description: Move among radical and rational-exponent forms, simplify exact values, and reject extraneous candidates.

routes.title: Exponential and logarithmic algebra repair
routes.description: Apply exponent and logarithm laws, convert between inverse forms, and solve basic equations with valid domains.

routes.title: Function notation and graph reading repair
routes.description: Evaluate functions, solve output conditions, and read domain, range, intercepts, extrema, and intervals from graphs.

routes.title: Mixed readiness synthesis
routes.description: Select methods across prerequisite strands, justify restrictions, and communicate exact and approximate results.

routes.title: Quantities, variables, and dependency
routes.description: Identify the input, output, parameters, and units in a quantitative relationship and explain how the quantities depend on one another.

routes.title: Relations and functions
routes.description: Determine whether a relation is a function by applying the rule that each allowed input has exactly one output.

routes.title: Function notation, evaluation, and solving
routes.description: Use function notation accurately and distinguish finding an output from finding inputs that produce a chosen output.

routes.title: Words, tables, graphs, and formulas
routes.description: Translate a function relationship among verbal, tabular, graphical, and algebraic representations while preserving quantities, units, and domain.

routes.title: Domain from formulas
routes.description: Determine the real domain of a function by combining denominator, even-root, logarithm, and composition restrictions.

routes.title: Domain from context
routes.description: Distinguish the algebraic domain of a formula from the inputs that are meaningful in a model.

routes.title: Range and global graph behavior
routes.description: Read range, intercepts, extrema, boundedness, symmetry, and intervals of increase or decrease from a graph.

routes.title: Piecewise-defined functions
routes.description: Evaluate, graph, and interpret functions that use different rules on different parts of the domain.

routes.title: Average rate of change
routes.description: Calculate and interpret average rate of change as output change per input change and as the slope of a secant line.

routes.title: Function representation and modeling studio
routes.description: Construct, compare, and defend function representations while stating assumptions, domain, units, and limitations.

routes.title: Parent-function atlas
routes.description: Recognize benchmark function families by domain, range, symmetry, intercepts, end behavior, and rate patterns.

routes.title: Coordinate mappings and transformation logic
routes.description: Derive graph transformations by tracking how input-output pairs move.

routes.title: Vertical translations
routes.description: Analyze how adding a constant outside a function changes outputs, range, intercepts, extrema, and asymptotes.

routes.title: Horizontal translations
routes.description: Analyze how replacing x by x-h changes input locations, domain, intercepts, extrema, and vertical asymptotes.

routes.title: Reflections and symmetry
routes.description: Reflect function graphs across coordinate axes and connect reflection rules with even and odd symmetry.

routes.title: Vertical and horizontal scaling
routes.description: Distinguish output scaling from input scaling and determine the resulting stretches, compressions, domains, and ranges.

routes.title: Combined transformations
routes.description: Analyze and graph functions with several transformations by tracking inputs, outputs, and key features.

routes.title: Sums and differences of functions
routes.description: Add and subtract functions pointwise, determine the common domain, and interpret combined outputs.

routes.title: Products and quotients of functions
routes.description: Multiply and divide functions pointwise while analyzing zeros, restrictions, and combined graph behavior.

routes.title: Reconstructing formulas from transformed graphs
routes.description: Use parent-family features, transformations, and one or more data points to construct and verify a function formula.

routes.title: Composition as sequential processing
routes.description: Interpret f composed with g as applying g first and then f, and explain why order generally matters.

routes.title: Composition from formulas
routes.description: Evaluate and simplify composite functions symbolically while preserving grouping and domain conditions.

routes.title: Composition from tables and graphs
routes.description: Evaluate composite functions when one or both functions are represented numerically or graphically.

routes.title: Domains of composite functions
routes.description: Determine the domain of a composite by enforcing both inner-function and outer-input conditions.

routes.title: One-to-one functions
routes.description: Determine whether a function is one-to-one and explain why one-to-one behavior is required for an inverse function.

routes.title: Constructing inverse functions
routes.description: Construct an inverse function algebraically and state the swapped domain and range.

routes.title: Graphs and verification of inverses
routes.description: Verify inverse functions using composition and graph symmetry across y=x.

routes.title: Domain restrictions and radical inverses
routes.description: Restrict power functions to one-to-one branches and connect those branches to principal radical functions.

routes.title: Model construction and validation
routes.description: Build a multi-stage function model, state its domain and assumptions, and evaluate whether an inverse interpretation is meaningful.

routes.title: Power functions and dominant behavior
routes.description: Compare power functions f(x)=ax^p and explain how exponent and coefficient control domain, symmetry, end behavior, and growth.

routes.title: Polynomial functions, degree, and leading term
routes.description: Identify degree, leading term, coefficients, and standard form, and explain why the leading term governs large-input behavior.

routes.title: End behavior
routes.description: Determine polynomial end behavior from degree parity and leading coefficient and express it verbally, graphically, and with limit-style notation.

routes.title: Zeros, factors, and intercepts
routes.description: Connect polynomial zeros, linear factors, solutions, and x-intercepts, and distinguish exact from approximate zeros.

routes.title: Multiplicity and sign behavior
routes.description: Relate the multiplicity of a zero to sign changes, crossing or touching behavior, and local flattening.

routes.title: Graph construction from structure
routes.description: Construct a polynomial graph from degree, leading coefficient, zeros, multiplicities, sign intervals, and selected points.

routes.title: Turning points and local versus global behavior
routes.description: Use degree bounds, graph evidence, and function values to analyze turning points and extrema.

routes.title: Intermediate Value reasoning and root bounds
routes.description: Use polynomial continuity and sign changes to guarantee roots and bracket them within intervals.

routes.title: Polynomial division
routes.description: Divide polynomials using long and synthetic division and verify the division algorithm P=DQ+R.

routes.title: Remainder and factor theorems
routes.description: Use P(c) as the remainder on division by x-c and test whether x-c is a factor.

routes.title: Rational-root candidates and root search
routes.description: Generate all possible rational zeros of an integer-coefficient polynomial and organize an efficient exact-and-numerical search.

routes.title: Complex zeros and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
routes.description: Count polynomial zeros over the complex numbers, use conjugate pairs for real coefficients, and build real polynomials from complex roots.

routes.title: Building polynomial models and finding numerical roots
routes.description: Construct polynomial functions from conditions, fit vertical scale, and approximate roots that lack convenient exact forms.

routes.title: Rational functions and their domains
routes.description: Identify rational functions and determine all excluded inputs from the original denominator before simplifying.

routes.title: Equivalent formulas, different functions, and holes
routes.description: Identify removable discontinuities caused by common factors and distinguish formula equivalence from function equality.

routes.title: Vertical asymptotes and local behavior
routes.description: Determine vertical asymptotes and describe one-sided behavior from factor signs and multiplicity.

routes.title: Horizontal asymptotes and end behavior
routes.description: Determine horizontal asymptotes from degree comparison and interpret them as long-run output behavior.

routes.title: Slant and polynomial asymptotes
routes.description: Use polynomial division to determine nonhorizontal asymptotes and describe the shrinking remainder term.

routes.title: Intercepts and sign charts
routes.description: Find rational intercepts and determine positive and negative intervals using factored sign structure.

routes.title: Complete rational graph construction
routes.description: Construct a complete rational graph using domain, discontinuities, asymptotes, intercepts, signs, and selected values.

routes.title: Rational equations and function intersections
routes.description: Solve rational equations and intersections exactly or numerically while rejecting excluded candidates.

routes.title: Rational inequalities
routes.description: Solve rational inequalities using critical values, sign intervals, and correct endpoint inclusion.

routes.title: Variation and rational models
routes.description: Build and interpret direct, inverse, joint, and combined variation models with meaningful parameters and domains.

routes.title: Partial-fraction structure
routes.description: Decompose proper rational functions with factorable denominators into simpler component fractions and verify recombination.

routes.title: Additive versus multiplicative change
routes.description: Distinguish linear, exponential, and neither patterns by comparing equal-input differences, ratios, and percent changes.

routes.title: Exponential functions and parameters
routes.description: Analyze f(x)=ab^x by interpreting initial value, base, multiplier, percent rate, domain, range, and asymptote.

routes.title: Exponential transformations
routes.description: Analyze transformed exponential functions and track asymptotes, domain, range, and feature points.

routes.title: Growth and decay models
routes.description: Construct exponential models from an initial value, rate, multiplier, two points, or a known doubling or half-life.

routes.title: Compound interest and effective rate
routes.description: Use periodic compounding models and compare nominal rates, periodic rates, compounding frequency, and effective annual yield.

routes.title: Continuous growth and the number e
routes.description: Use A(t)=A0e^(kt) for continuous proportional change and interpret the continuous rate parameter k.

routes.title: Exponential regression and residuals
routes.description: Fit an exponential model to data, interpret parameters, inspect residuals, and evaluate interpolation and extrapolation.

routes.title: Logistic and bounded growth
routes.description: Analyze logistic growth qualitatively and interpret initial value, carrying capacity, growth rate, and inflection behavior.

routes.title: Logarithms as inverse functions
routes.description: Define log base b as the inverse of b^x, convert between forms, and interpret logarithms as exponents.

routes.title: Logarithmic graphs and transformations
routes.description: Analyze transformed logarithmic functions, including domain, range, vertical asymptote, intercepts, and base-dependent direction.

routes.title: Logarithm laws
routes.description: Derive and apply product, quotient, and power laws while preserving positive-argument domains.

routes.title: Solving exponential equations
routes.description: Solve exponential equations using common bases, logarithms, and numerical methods, and interpret exact and approximate answers.

routes.title: Solving logarithmic equations and interpreting inverse models
routes.description: Solve logarithmic equations, reject invalid arguments, and use logarithms to analyze doubling time, half-life, and logarithmic scales.

routes.title: Systems as intersections and models
routes.description: Interpret a system solution as an input-output point satisfying every equation and solve two-variable systems graphically and algebraically.

routes.title: Nonlinear systems
routes.description: Solve systems involving lines, quadratics, circles, rational, exponential, or other nonlinear functions and interpret all real intersections.

routes.title: Systems of inequalities and feasible regions
routes.description: Graph simultaneous inequalities, identify feasible regions, and interpret boundaries and vertices.

routes.title: Systems in three variables
routes.description: Solve and classify three-variable linear systems and interpret their solutions as intersections of planes.

routes.title: Matrix notation and operations
routes.description: Represent rectangular arrays with matrices and perform dimension-compatible addition, scalar multiplication, and matrix multiplication.

routes.title: Augmented matrices and row operations
routes.description: Translate linear systems into augmented matrices and justify elementary row operations as equivalent-system transformations.

routes.title: Gaussian elimination and echelon form
routes.description: Use forward elimination to reach row-echelon form and solve by back-substitution.

routes.title: Gauss-Jordan elimination and reduced row-echelon form
routes.description: Reduce matrices to RREF and interpret pivots, free variables, rank, and consistency directly.

routes.title: Determinants, singularity, and inverse matrices
routes.description: Compute and interpret determinants, identify singular matrices, and solve suitable systems with inverse matrices.

routes.title: Linear transformations and multivariable modeling
routes.description: Interpret matrices as transformations of vectors and construct a complete multivariable model using equations, inequalities, and matrices.

routes.title: Directed rotation and coterminal angles
routes.description: Represent rotations in standard position and generate all coterminal angles.

routes.title: Degree measure and angular coordinates
routes.description: Use degrees, revolutions, and degree-minute-second notation to measure and compare rotation.

routes.title: Radian measure as normalized arc length
routes.description: Define radian measure as signed arc length divided by radius and explain why it is independent of circle size.

routes.title: Arc length and sector area
routes.description: Derive and use s=r theta and A=(1/2)r^2 theta for angles measured in radians.

routes.title: Angular speed and linear speed
routes.description: Relate angular speed, radius, and tangential speed using v=r omega.

routes.title: Wrapping the real line around the unit circle
routes.description: Map any real number t to the unit-circle point reached by signed arc length t.

routes.title: Sine and cosine as coordinate functions
routes.description: Define cosine and sine as the x- and y-coordinates of the unit-circle point P(t).

routes.title: Exact values from special triangles
routes.description: Derive exact unit-circle values from 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.

routes.title: Reference angles, quadrants, and signs
routes.description: Use reference angles and quadrant signs to evaluate trigonometric functions of arbitrary rotations.

routes.title: Tangent and the reciprocal functions
routes.description: Define tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant from sine and cosine and state domains, signs, periods, and identities.

routes.title: Building the sine graph from circular motion
routes.description: Construct y=sin t from the vertical coordinate of a rotating unit-circle point.

routes.title: Building the cosine graph from circular motion
routes.description: Construct y=cos t from the horizontal coordinate of circular motion and compare it with sine.

routes.title: Amplitude, reflection, and midline
routes.description: Interpret A and D in y=A sin x+D or y=A cos x+D.

routes.title: Period, frequency, and angular frequency
routes.description: Relate inside scale B to period, ordinary frequency, and angular frequency.

routes.title: Phase shift and timing
routes.description: Interpret B(x-C) as a horizontal timing shift and recover C from graph or context.

routes.title: The general sinusoidal function
routes.description: Build and analyze y=A sin(B(x-C))+D and equivalent cosine forms.

routes.title: Tangent and cotangent graphs
routes.description: Derive tangent and cotangent graphs from quotient definitions, zeros, asymptotes, and period pi.

routes.title: Secant and cosecant graphs
routes.description: Construct secant and cosecant graphs as reciprocals of cosine and sine.

routes.title: Symmetry, periodicity, and the six-function family
routes.description: Compare domains, ranges, parity, periods, zeros, and asymptotes of all six trig functions.

routes.title: Inverse trigonometric functions and branch restrictions
routes.description: Define inverse sine, cosine, and tangent using one-to-one branches and principal-value ranges.

routes.title: Basic trigonometric equations
routes.description: Solve sin x=k, cos x=k, and tan x=k using exact values, inverse functions, periodicity, and interval restrictions.

routes.title: Sinusoidal modeling and regression
routes.description: Fit and critique sinusoidal models using amplitude, midline, period, phase, residuals, and domain.

routes.title: Identities, equations, and proof strategy
routes.description: Distinguish identities from conditional equations and use valid one-sided transformation strategies.

routes.title: Reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean identities
routes.description: Derive and apply the fundamental trig identities from unit-circle coordinates.

routes.title: Verifying identities strategically
routes.description: Select factoring, common denominators, conjugates, or sine-cosine conversion to verify identities.

routes.title: Sum and difference formulas
routes.description: Derive and apply sine, cosine, and tangent sum and difference formulas.

routes.title: Double-angle formulas
routes.description: Derive and use double-angle identities, including three equivalent cosine forms.

routes.title: Half-angle and power-reduction formulas
routes.description: Derive half-angle and power-reduction identities and select signs using quadrant information.

routes.title: Product-to-sum and sum-to-product formulas
routes.description: Convert products and sums of trig functions to alternate forms and interpret signal combinations.

routes.title: Equations using fundamental identities
routes.description: Solve trig equations by converting functions, factoring, and applying fundamental identities.

routes.title: Quadratic-form trigonometric equations
routes.description: Use substitution and algebraic solving for equations quadratic in a trig function.

routes.title: Multiple-angle equations
routes.description: Solve equations involving sin(nx), cos(nx), or tan(nx) and translate solution families back to x.

routes.title: General solutions and interval restrictions
routes.description: Write complete periodic solution families and extract all solutions from specified intervals.

routes.title: Exact and numerical trigonometric equation solving
routes.description: Use graphing, bracketing, and numerical methods for trig equations without convenient exact solutions.

routes.title: Right triangles and trigonometric ratios
routes.description: Connect unit-circle trig definitions with ratios in similar right triangles.

routes.title: Right-triangle applications
routes.description: Model heights, distances, slopes, and angles of elevation or depression.

routes.title: The Law of Sines
routes.description: Derive and apply the Law of Sines to ASA, AAS, and suitable SSA triangles.

routes.title: The ambiguous SSA case
routes.description: Determine whether SSA data produce zero, one, or two triangles.

routes.title: The Law of Cosines
routes.description: Use the Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS data and connect it to the Pythagorean theorem.

routes.title: Triangle area formulas
routes.description: Use K=(1/2)ab sin C and compare with base-height and Heron forms.

routes.title: Bearings and navigation
routes.description: Translate among standard angles, quadrant bearings, headings, and triangle or component models.

routes.title: Vectors geometrically and in components
routes.description: Represent vectors by magnitude and direction, add them geometrically, and convert to components.

routes.title: Vector operations, magnitude, direction, and unit vectors
routes.description: Use scalar multiplication, normalization, and component resolution.

routes.title: Dot product, angles, and projection
routes.description: Use the dot product to find angles, test orthogonality, and calculate projections.

routes.title: Conics as loci and the circle foundation
routes.description: Define loci by distance conditions and derive the standard circle equation.

routes.title: Parabolas from focus and directrix
routes.description: Derive and analyze parabolas as points equidistant from a focus and directrix.

routes.title: Ellipses
routes.description: Analyze ellipses from constant-sum distance and standard equations.

routes.title: Hyperbolas
routes.description: Analyze hyperbolas from constant-difference distance and standard equations.

routes.title: Completing squares in two variables
routes.description: Convert general quadratic relations to standard conic form by completing squares.

routes.title: Translated conics and general equations
routes.description: Classify translated conics and recover all geometric features from standard form.

routes.title: Degenerate conics and classification
routes.description: Identify point, line, pair-of-lines, empty-set, and other degenerate quadratic relations.

routes.title: Eccentricity and unified conic structure
routes.description: Use eccentricity to compare circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.

routes.title: Nonlinear systems involving conics
routes.description: Solve and interpret intersections of lines, circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas.

routes.title: Conic models and applications
routes.description: Construct and critique conic models in reflection, orbit, architecture, and navigation settings.

routes.title: Parametric equations and orientation
routes.description: Interpret x=f(t), y=g(t) as a directed path with a parameter interval.

routes.title: Eliminating a parameter
routes.description: Eliminate parameters while preserving interval restrictions and lost orientation information.

routes.title: Parametric motion and vector-valued position
routes.description: Use r(t)=<x(t),y(t)> to describe position, displacement, and average velocity.

routes.title: Intersections, repeated points, and multiple parameter values
routes.description: Distinguish curve intersections from self-intersections and repeated positions.

routes.title: Polar coordinates and nonuniqueness
routes.description: Represent points as (r,theta), use negative radius, and generate equivalent polar coordinates.

routes.title: Cartesian and polar conversion
routes.description: Convert points and equations using x=r cos theta, y=r sin theta, and r^2=x^2+y^2.

routes.title: Graphing polar equations
routes.description: Trace r=f(theta) using tables, signed radius, and interval selection.

routes.title: Polar symmetry and repeated tracing
routes.description: Test symmetry and choose intervals that trace a polar curve exactly once.

routes.title: Common polar families and polar conics
routes.description: Analyze parameter effects in circles, cardioids, limacons, roses, lemniscates, spirals, and conics.

routes.title: Complex numbers in polar form
routes.description: Represent complex numbers by modulus and argument and convert between rectangular and polar forms.

routes.title: Complex multiplication, division, and powers
routes.description: Multiply moduli, add arguments, divide moduli, subtract arguments, and apply De Moivre's theorem.

routes.title: Roots of complex numbers
routes.description: Find all nth roots of a complex number and interpret their equal angular spacing.

routes.title: Sequences as discrete functions
routes.description: Interpret a sequence as a function on an integer index set.

routes.title: Explicit and recursive descriptions
routes.description: Move among term lists, explicit formulas, recursive rules, tables, and plots.

routes.title: Arithmetic sequences
routes.description: Derive and use a_n=a_1+(n-1)d and connect arithmetic sequences to sampled linear functions.

routes.title: Geometric sequences
routes.description: Derive and use a_n=a_1r^{n-1} and connect geometric sequences to sampled exponential functions.

routes.title: Recurrence, iteration, and discrete dynamical models
routes.description: Analyze repeated function application, fixed points, cycles, and qualitative long-run behavior.

routes.title: Sigma notation and finite sums
routes.description: Interpret summation notation, index bounds, summands, and term counts.

routes.title: Arithmetic series
routes.description: Derive and use S_n=n(a_1+a_n)/2.

routes.title: Finite geometric series
routes.description: Derive and use S_n=a_1(1-r^n)/(1-r).

routes.title: Infinite geometric series and convergence
routes.description: Determine convergence and evaluate infinite geometric sums when |r|<1.

routes.title: Mathematical induction
routes.description: Prove statements for all integers in a domain using base case and inductive step.

routes.title: Pascal's triangle and binomial coefficients
routes.description: Connect combinations, recursive construction, symmetry, and polynomial coefficients.

routes.title: The binomial theorem and discrete-model synthesis
routes.description: Expand binomial powers and compare arithmetic, geometric, recursive, and accumulated models.

routes.title: Function-family classification
routes.description: Classify unfamiliar formulas, graphs, tables, and contexts using structural evidence.

routes.title: Model selection and comparison
routes.description: Select and compare function models using patterns, residuals, domains, and parameter meanings.

routes.title: Average rate of change revisited
routes.description: Compare average rates across function families and interpret units and interval dependence.

routes.title: Difference quotients
routes.description: Construct and simplify [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h and interpret its components.

routes.title: Secant lines and tangent intuition
routes.description: Interpret tangent slope as a limiting value of secant slopes.

routes.title: Local linearity and magnification
routes.description: Recognize when a smooth graph appears linear under magnification and identify failures of local linearity.

routes.title: Intuitive limits
routes.description: Estimate limits from tables, graphs, and algebra while distinguishing approached value from function value.

routes.title: Continuity and discontinuity
routes.description: Classify removable, jump, infinite, and endpoint discontinuities using function values and limiting behavior.

routes.title: Infinite behavior and asymptotes
routes.description: Synthesize finite and infinite input behavior across polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric families.

routes.title: Numerical approximation and sensitivity
routes.description: Use bracketing, iteration, finite differences, and residuals while evaluating sensitivity to rounding and parameter error.

routes.title: Accumulation, finite sums, and area preview
routes.description: Connect rates, rectangles, finite sums, net change, and area under a rate graph.

routes.title: Precalculus synthesis capstone
routes.description: Analyze an unfamiliar multirepresentation problem by selecting and combining methods from the entire course.
